cards.q: What does sizeof(int*) give in a 64-bit program, and why does it not depend on what the pointer points at?
cards.a: 8. A pointer holds an address, and every address in a 64-bit program takes 8 bytes.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Is a Row of Bytes

cards.q: Why do the addresses printed change every time the program runs?
cards.a: Windows loads the program, stack and heap at random positions each time (ASLR). The layout inside stays the same; the starting point moves.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Is a Row of Bytes

cards.q: An int holding 0x0A0B0C0D is stored at address 0x500 on a little-endian machine. What byte is at 0x500?
cards.a: 0x0D, the least significant byte. The bytes from 0x500 up are 0D 0C 0B 0A.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Is a Row of Bytes

cards.q: Why must a char* be cast to void* before printing it with std::cout?
cards.a: std::cout treats char* as text and prints characters until a zero byte. void* prints as an address.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Is a Row of Bytes

cards.q: int* p{ &score }; What is the value stored in p, and what is the value of &p?
cards.a: p holds score's address. &p is the address of p itself, a different place in memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses

cards.q: In int* a, b; what type is b?
cards.a: A plain int. The star applies to a only.
cards.lessonTitle: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses

cards.q: Why will the compiler not let an int* hold the address of a double?
cards.a: The pointer's type says how to read the bytes at the address. Reading a double's bytes as an int is meaningless, so the conversion needs an explicit cast.
cards.lessonTitle: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses

cards.q: int a{ 5 }, b{ 5 }; Is &a == &b?
cards.a: No. They hold equal values but are two different objects at two different addresses.
cards.lessonTitle: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses

cards.q: int x{ 3 }; int* p{ &x }; *p = *p * 2; What is x?
cards.a: 6. *p is x itself.

cards.q: What is the difference between p->hp and *p.hp?
cards.a: p->hp means (*p).hp, the member of the struct p points at. *p.hp tries to take member hp of the pointer and then dereference it, which does not compile for a plain pointer.

cards.q: Which of these compile? const int* a; *a = 1; and int* const b{ &x }; *b = 1;
cards.a: Only the second. a points at a const int so cannot write through it; b is a const pointer but the int it points at can change.

cards.q: Two pointers p and q hold the same address. *p = 9; What is *q?
cards.a: 9. They reach the same object.

cards.q: Why does void heal(int h) { h += 25; } not change the caller's variable?
cards.a: The argument is copied into h. The function changes its copy, which disappears when it returns.

cards.q: heal(int* h) is called with heal(&health). Is the pointer copied?
cards.a: Yes, but the copy holds the same address, so *h reaches the caller's health.

cards.q: When is a pointer parameter better than a reference parameter?
cards.a: When "no object" is meaningful and the caller may pass nullptr, or when the function is a C-style interface.

cards.q: A function writes *countOut = n; and the documentation says countOut is optional. What is missing?
cards.a: A null check: if (countOut) *countOut = n;

cards.q: A crash says "read access violation, p was 0x10". What most likely happened?
cards.a: p was nullptr and the code read the member at offset 0x10 of the struct it was supposed to point at.

cards.q: Why is a dangling pointer harder to find than a null pointer?
cards.a: Its address is still mapped and often still holds the old value, so following it seems to work until the memory is reused, and the crash appears far from the bug.

cards.q: In an MSVC debug build a pointer shows the value 0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD. What does that tell you?
cards.a: The pointer itself was read from heap memory that had been freed: the object holding it was already deleted.

cards.q: Why is keeping a pointer to v[0] across v.push_back risky?
cards.a: push_back may move all the elements to a new, larger block and free the old one, leaving the pointer dangling.

cards.q: An array of double starts at 0x2000. Where is element 3?
Inside void f(int values[10]), what is sizeof(values) on 64-bit Windows?
cards.a: 8, the size of a pointer. The array decayed and the 10 is ignored.

cards.q: Why do C-style functions take a count alongside the array?
cards.a: The function receives only the address of the first element; the length is lost when the array decays.

cards.q: What does values[i] mean in terms of pointers?
cards.a: *(values + i): move i elements along from values and follow the address.

cards.q: double* d points at 0x1000. What address is d + 3?
cards.a: 0x1018: three doubles of 8 bytes each.

cards.q: int* a = &v[2]; int* b = &v[9]; What is b - a?
cards.a: 7 elements.

cards.q: Why is end = begin + count allowed but *end is not?
cards.a: The one-past-the-end pointer may be computed and compared, but there is no element there to read.

cards.q: You need the address 6 bytes after an int* p. How do you compute it?
cards.a: Through a byte pointer: reinterpret_cast<unsigned char*>(p) + 6. p + 6 would be 24 bytes on.

cards.q: How many bytes does the string literal "pointer" take?
cards.a: 8: seven characters and the terminating zero.

cards.q: Why does a find function return end instead of nullptr for "not found"?
cards.a: end is always a valid position in the range to compare against, and it lets the caller search any sub-range in the same way.

cards.q: What does strcpy do if the destination array is too small?
cards.a: It keeps writing past the end of the destination until it has copied the source's zero byte, corrupting whatever follows.

cards.q: A function stores s.c_str() from a std::string parameter passed by value. What is wrong?
cards.a: The parameter is destroyed when the function returns, so the stored pointer dangles.

cards.q: A grid is 10 wide and 6 high, stored row-major. What is the index of column 3, row 4?
An image is 100 pixels wide with a stride of 128 pixels. Where does pixel (0, 1) start, counted in pixels from the top-left?
cards.a: At 128, not 100: one stride on.

cards.q: An image comes out slanted, each row shifted a little more than the last. What is the likely bug?
cards.a: The code used the width where it should have used the stride (or mixed bytes and pixels).

cards.q: Why is a sub-view cheap?
cards.a: It is only a new start pointer, width and height with the same stride; it shares the original memory instead of copying it.

cards.q: Why is *reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&someFloat) wrong even though it usually prints the right bits?
cards.a: It breaks the strict aliasing rule, so the behaviour is undefined: optimised builds may reorder or drop the read.

cards.q: Which types may legally view the bytes of any object?
cards.a: char, unsigned char and std::byte.

cards.q: How do you read a 4-byte number stored at offset 6 of a byte buffer?
cards.a: std::memcpy(&value, buffer + 6, 4), or assemble it from the four bytes with shifts. A pointer cast is both an aliasing violation and a misaligned read.

cards.q: Which cast turns an address into a plain integer?
cards.a: reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(pointer).

cards.q: An Enemy pointer holds 0x5000 and health is at offset 12. What address does enemy->health read?
struct S { char a; int b; char c; }; What is sizeof(S), and why?
cards.a: 12. a at 0, three bytes of padding, b at 4, c at 8, and three bytes of trailing padding so the size is a multiple of 4.

cards.q: How can that struct be made smaller?
cards.a: Put the int first: int b; char a; char c; gives offsets 0, 4, 5 and size 8.

cards.q: Why should a struct not be compared with memcmp?
cards.a: Its padding bytes have unspecified contents, so two structs with equal members can still differ byte for byte.

cards.q: int x{ 1 }; int* p{ &x }; int** pp{ &p }; What are *pp and **pp?
cards.a: *pp is p (the address of x); **pp is x, 1.

cards.q: Why does a function that creates an object for the caller often take Thing** out?
cards.a: It needs to change the caller's pointer variable, so it needs that variable's address.

cards.q: In the pointer-to-pointer removal, why is the first node not a special case?
cards.a: link may point at head or at any node's next; assigning *link updates whichever pointer pointed at the removed node.

cards.q: What is argv[argc]?
cards.a: nullptr: the array of argument pointers ends with a null pointer.

cards.q: In the chain base -> 0x00 -> 0x00 -> 0x08 -> 0x10 -> 0x04, why is the last offset added without a read?
cards.a: The last step gives the address of the value itself; every earlier step reads a pointer to the next object.

cards.q: Why must a chain be checked for nullptr at every step?
cards.a: Any object along the path may not exist at that moment; reading through its null pointer would crash.

cards.q: Why does the address of health change between runs while the chain stays the same?
cards.a: Heap allocations and the program's load address change every run, but the struct offsets are compiled in and the first link is anchored to a global at a fixed offset inside the program.

cards.q: Where does offset 0x08 in the World step come from?
cards.a: From the struct layout: offsetof(World, players), after the int tick and 4 bytes of padding.

cards.q: Why does inserting into the middle of a linked list not depend on its length?
cards.a: Only the pointers of the neighbouring nodes change; nothing has to move.

cards.q: Why is walking a linked list usually much slower than walking a vector with the same values?
cards.a: The nodes are scattered in memory, so almost every step is a cache miss, while a vector is read sequentially.

cards.q: What does a sentinel node remove from a doubly linked list's code?
cards.a: All the nullptr checks and special cases for the first and last nodes: every real node always has a real prev and next.

cards.q: In an intrusive list, how do you get from a pointer to the embedded links back to the whole object?
cards.a: Subtract the links member's offset from its address (what CONTAINING_RECORD does).

cards.q: What does int (*f)(double) declare?
cards.a: f is a pointer to a function that takes a double and returns an int.

cards.q: Why do C-style callback APIs take a void* context argument?
cards.a: A plain function pointer carries no data, so the caller's state travels separately as a void* that the library hands back unchanged.

cards.q: What happens, step by step, in a virtual call unit->attack()?
cards.a: Read the vtable pointer from the object, read attack's address from its slot in the table, call that address.

cards.q: Which lambdas can be passed where a plain function pointer is expected?
cards.a: Lambdas with no captures.

cards.q: Is it safe for a function to return a const char* pointing at the literal "error"?
cards.a: Yes. String literals have static storage and live for the whole program.

cards.q: When is a static local variable initialised?
cards.a: The first time execution passes its declaration; after that it keeps its value between calls.

cards.q: A function creates a 4 MB array as a local variable. What is likely to happen?
cards.a: A stack overflow: the default stack is 1 MB. Use a std::vector, which keeps its elements on the heap.

cards.q: Which storage duration does the inside of a std::vector have?
cards.a: Dynamic: the vector object can be a local, but its elements are allocated on the heap.

cards.q: Does the stack pointer go up or down when a function is called on x64?
cards.a: Down: the new frame is at lower addresses than the caller's.

cards.q: Why might printing through a pointer to a dead local still show the old value?
cards.a: Returning only moves the stack pointer; the bytes stay until another call reuses that part of the stack.

cards.q: What is the default stack size of a thread on Windows, and what happens when it runs out?
cards.a: 1 MB. Touching the guard page beyond it raises a stack overflow exception and the program ends.

cards.q: What does the /GS security cookie protect?
cards.a: The return address: a random value between the locals and the return address is checked before returning, so an overrun that reaches the return address is caught.

cards.q: What two things does new Enemy{...} do?
cards.a: Get memory from the allocator, then run Enemy's constructor in it.

cards.q: Why does delete need no size?
cards.a: The allocator stores the block's size in a header next to the block.

cards.q: Writing one int past the end of a heap array often does nothing visible at first. Why does it crash later?
cards.a: It overwrites the next block's header; the damage is noticed only when the allocator next uses that header.

cards.q: What is wrong with int* a = new int[8]; delete a;?
cards.a: An array allocated with new[] must be freed with delete[].

cards.q: Two parts of a program both delete the same object. Which rule was broken?
cards.a: The object had two owners; every heap object must have exactly one.

cards.q: A function's documentation says "the returned string must be freed with LocalFree". Who owns the string?
cards.a: The caller, from the moment the function returns, and it must free it with LocalFree specifically.

cards.q: Destroying a std::vector<Enemy*> frees what?
cards.a: Only the vector's own array of pointers, not the enemies they point at.

cards.q: Why should a class that owns raw pointers delete its copy constructor?
cards.a: The default copy copies the pointers, giving two owners that would both delete the same objects.

cards.q: Why is a leak in a long-running game more serious than in a short command-line tool?
cards.a: Windows reclaims everything when a program exits, but a game that leaks a little every frame keeps growing for hours until it slows down or runs out of memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Leaks and How to Find Them

cards.q: The leak report shows {157} normal block. How do you find the code that allocated it?
cards.a: Call _CrtSetBreakAlloc(157) at the start of main and run again; the debugger stops when allocation 157 happens.
cards.lessonTitle: Leaks and How to Find Them

cards.q: A leaked block's data shows CD CD CD CD. What does that tell you?
cards.a: The block was allocated but never written to.
cards.lessonTitle: Leaks and How to Find Them

cards.q: Name two bugs AddressSanitizer reports at the moment they happen.
cards.a: Any of: heap, stack or global buffer overflow, use after free, use after return, double free, mismatched new[]/delete.
cards.lessonTitle: Leaks and How to Find Them

cards.q: What does C++ guarantee that makes RAII work?
cards.a: An object's destructor runs whenever it goes out of scope, including through return, break and exceptions.

cards.q: Two RAII objects a and b are created in that order in one scope. Which is destroyed first?
cards.a: b. Destruction runs in reverse order of creation.

cards.q: Why must an RAII class that wraps a FILE* do something about copying?
cards.a: The default copy would copy the pointer, so two objects would both close the same file.

cards.q: What is a scope guard's dismiss() for?
cards.a: Cancelling the clean-up action, for commit-or-roll-back code: dismiss only once the work succeeded.

cards.q: Why can a std::unique_ptr not be copied?
cards.a: It is the sole owner; a copy would create two owners that both delete the object.

cards.q: After auto b = std::move(a); with a a unique_ptr, what does a hold?
cards.a: nullptr: ownership moved to b.

cards.q: What is the difference between p.reset() and p.release()?
cards.a: reset deletes the object and leaves p empty; release gives up ownership without deleting and returns the raw pointer for someone else to free.

cards.q: How do you make a unique_ptr that closes a FILE* instead of deleting it?
cards.a: Give it a custom deleter: a struct whose operator() calls fclose, as the second template argument.

cards.q: When does a shared_ptr delete its object?
cards.a: When the last shared_ptr owning it is destroyed or reset, so the strong count reaches zero.

cards.q: Why is std::make_shared better than shared_ptr<T>(new T)?
cards.a: It allocates the object and the control block in one heap block instead of two.

cards.q: Two objects hold shared_ptrs to each other. What happens when everything else lets go of them?
cards.a: Neither count reaches zero, so both leak.

cards.q: How do you use the object a weak_ptr refers to?
cards.a: Call lock(); it returns a shared_ptr that is empty if the object is gone.

cards.q: What does a std::span hold?
cards.a: A pointer to the first element and the number of elements.

cards.q: Why is a std::span passed by value rather than by reference?
cards.a: It is only 16 bytes, a pointer and a size, so copying it is as cheap as passing a reference.

cards.q: Why must you not pass a string_view's data() to a C function expecting a C string?
cards.a: A string_view need not be followed by a zero byte, so the function would read past its end.

cards.q: A span views a vector, then the vector has elements pushed onto it. What can go wrong?
cards.a: The vector may move its elements to a new block, leaving the span pointing at freed memory.

cards.q: What goes wrong when a class owning a raw new[] array uses the default copy constructor?
cards.a: Both objects hold the same pointer, so both destructors delete the same array.
cards.lessonTitle: Copy and Move for Owning Types

cards.q: What must a move constructor do to the object it moved from?
cards.a: Leave it valid but empty, typically setting its pointer to nullptr, so its destructor frees nothing.
cards.lessonTitle: Copy and Move for Owning Types

cards.q: Why should a move constructor be noexcept?
cards.a: std::vector only moves elements when growing if the move cannot throw; otherwise it copies them.
cards.lessonTitle: Copy and Move for Owning Types

cards.q: What is the rule of zero?
cards.a: If every member manages its own resource, the class needs no destructor and no copy or move functions of its own.
cards.lessonTitle: Copy and Move for Owning Types

cards.q: Why does an allocator split a large free block?
cards.a: So a small request does not use up the whole block; the rest stays available as a smaller free block.

cards.q: What is fragmentation?
cards.a: Free memory scattered in many small blocks between used ones, so a large request can fail even though enough memory is free in total.

cards.q: Where are the next pointers of a free list stored?
cards.a: Inside the free blocks themselves, since their memory is not in use.

cards.q: What does (value + 15) & ~15 do?
cards.a: Rounds value up to the next multiple of 16.

cards.q: What does allocating from an arena cost?
cards.a: Rounding the offset up for alignment, one comparison against the end, and one addition.

cards.q: Why is an arena a good fit for per-frame memory in a game?
cards.a: Everything allocated during a frame dies at the end of the frame, so one reset frees all of it at once.

cards.q: What does rewinding to a marker free?
cards.a: Everything allocated after the marker was taken; earlier allocations stay.

cards.q: Why should objects in an arena be trivially destructible?
cards.a: reset does not call destructors, so anything that owns other resources would leak them.

cards.q: Why does a pool allocator have no fragmentation?
cards.a: Every block is the same size, so any free block satisfies any request.

cards.q: Where does the pool keep the list of free blocks?
cards.a: As a linked list whose next pointers are stored in the first bytes of the free blocks themselves.

cards.q: Why must each block be at least sizeof(void*) bytes?
cards.a: A free block has to hold the pointer to the next free block.

cards.q: Why do use-after-free bugs on pooled objects show up quickly?
cards.a: The freed block's first bytes are overwritten by the free-list pointer at once, and the block is the next one handed out.

cards.q: For the address 0x12345, what are the page number and the offset with 4 KB pages?
cards.a: Page 0x12, offset 0x345.

cards.q: What is the difference between reserving and committing memory?
cards.a: Reserving sets aside a range of addresses with no memory behind it; committing backs pages with memory so they can be accessed.

cards.q: Why does every null pointer dereference fault immediately on Windows?
cards.a: The lowest 64 KB of the address space is never mapped, so any address near 0 has no translation.

cards.q: How does page heap catch a buffer overrun at the exact instruction?
cards.a: It puts each allocation at the end of a page with an inaccessible page after it, so the first byte past the end faults.

cards.q: A crash reports reading address 0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDE5. What happened?
cards.a: A pointer was read out of freed heap memory (the DD fill) and then a member at offset 8 was accessed: a use after free one level removed.
cards.lessonTitle: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs

cards.q: Something overwrites a struct's field and you cannot see where. Which debugger feature finds the culprit?
cards.a: A data breakpoint on the field's address, which stops at the instruction that writes to it.
cards.lessonTitle: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs

cards.q: What do AddressSanitizer, page heap and the debug heap's patterns have in common?
cards.a: They make a memory bug fail at, or near, the moment of the mistake instead of later.
cards.lessonTitle: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs

cards.q: A program works in a Debug build but crashes in Release. Name two likely causes.
cards.a: Any two of: an uninitialised variable, undefined behaviour the optimiser exploited, a strict aliasing violation, a timing-dependent dangling pointer.
cards.lessonTitle: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs
